summary: Reviewed 4 files (FilterExpressionParser.cs, FilterExpressionEvaluator.cs, FilterExpressionParserTests.cs, FilterExpressionEvaluatorTests.cs). 0 Critical, 0 High, 0 Medium, 0 Low. 1 Info (unbounded parser recursion depth). DSL uses strict identifier allowlisting; evaluator is pure in-memory with no external I/O or SQL construction from DSL input. Security sign-off: PASS \u2014 cleanest of the three WPs.

comments.note: No security findings — all OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed; no Critical or High issues identified. FilterExpressionParser enforces a strict allowlist (NumericIdentifiers + FunctionIdentifiers HashSets with OrdinalIgnoreCase comparison) — any unrecognised identifier throws FilterExpressionException at parse time, preventing unknown DSL terms from reaching the evaluator. FilterExpressionEvaluator operates entirely in-memory against MovieListItem objects; no SQL is constructed from DSL expressions, eliminating any injection path from the DSL to the database. EvaluateBookmarkContains validates argument count and type (StringLiteralNode) before performing a safe OrdinalIgnoreCase in-memory Contains check.

INFO | A04 — Insecure Design (unbounded recursion) | File: src/VideoIndexer.Core/Filtering/FilterExpressionParser.cs, ParsePrimaryExpression (line 156). The recursive-descent parser has no maximum nesting depth guard. An expression with extremely deep parenthesis nesting (e.g., '(((((...))))') could exhaust the call stack with a StackOverflowException. This is an Info-level finding only because: (1) this is a desktop app where the user types their own filter expressions; (2) there is no remote attack surface. Remediation: add a depth counter to the parser and throw FilterExpressionException when a configurable limit (e.g., 64 levels) is reached, to provide a graceful error instead of a process crash.

FilterExpressionParser: M7Identifiers and M10Identifiers are both empty sets. The developer left them in place intentionally as documentation placeholders (with accurate comments noting they are now empty). Keeping them avoids merge conflicts if future milestones need to re-introduce deferred identifiers via the same pattern. No action required.

FilterExpressionEvaluator: EvaluateBookmarkContains uses item.BookmarkDescriptions.Any(...) assuming BookmarkDescriptions is never null. Consistent with other collection-backed evaluators (e.g. EffectiveTagIds). If MovieListItem can be constructed with a null BookmarkDescriptions, this would throw a NullReferenceException at eval time. Recommend confirming the model initialises BookmarkDescriptions to an empty collection by default.

FilterExpressionParser.ParseArgumentList handles only 0 or 1 argument. This is intentional (documented in the comment). BookmarkContains requires exactly 1 arg and the evaluator enforces this with a runtime check. Pattern is consistent with other single-arg functions (ActorsContain, StudioContains, HasTag, TagHasSubTags). No issue.

The recursive-descent parser has no maximum nesting depth guard. For the desktop-app context (user-typed filter expressions) this is an Info-level concern only — a StackOverflowException requires extremely deep parenthesis nesting. Consider adding a depth counter and throwing FilterExpressionException at a configurable limit (e.g. 64 levels) as a polish item.
